title: Grand Unified Grammar of Graphics (GUGOG)
text:
Declarative, modular, and compositional approaches to visualization specification—collectively known as graphical or visualization grammars—have proliferated across visualization research and practice. However, despite sharing intellectual roots in Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics, these systems differ substantially in their abstractions, primitives, design goals, and target users.
GUGOG is a half-day hybrid workshop at IEEE VIS 2026 that brings together researchers and practitioners working on grammar-based visualization to seek a unified view of this diverse landscape. The workshop provides a dedicated forum for cross-system comparison, meta-theoretical reflection, community consensus building, and practitioner perspectives—structured opportunities that the main conference program rarely affords.
Read the full workshop proposal here.
GUGOG is held in conjunction with IEEE VIS 2026 and co-organized with the Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML).

title: Grand Unified Grammar of Graphics (GUGOG)
section: Panel: Towards a Universal Visualisation Language
text:
Panel: Towards a Universal Visualisation Language

Grammar-based systems all trace their lineage to Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics, yet they diverge sharply in their primitives, composition rules, design goals, and intended users. This panel asks the question that motivates the workshop: is a universal visualisation language a coherent goal, or does the diversity of grammars reflect genuine differences in what people need to express?
Panellists will draw on their own experience building and studying grammars and languages for visualisation to consider what a shared foundation would have to account for — interaction, computation and data access, diagrams beyond statistical charts, and the practicalities of learnability and adoption — and where unification would cost more than it gains. The discussion opens the landscape for the breakout sessions that follow in the afternoon.
Moderated by Cynthia Huang.







Andrew McNutt is currently an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Utah, and an incoming professor at the University of British Columbia. His group builds tools, develops theories, and conduct studies that turn domain expertise (such as for making charts) into software that is approachable, trustworthy, and respectful of user agency. The work spans HCI, visualization, and programming interfaces. He has won multiple paper awards at HCI and visualization venues, received the Johanna Beyer EuroVis Early Career Award, and was a Siebel Scholar. mcnutt.in









Eugene Wu is an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University and Co-director of the new Data, Agents, and Processes Lab (DAPLab). He is broadly interested in the foundations of computing infrastructure that are needed in a future where AI agents can safely, reliably, and efficiently automate complex work. His research spans the computing stack, from visualization and HCI to core data systems. Eugene has received the VLDB 2018 10-year test of time award, best-of-conference citations at ICDE and VLDB, the NSF CAREER, and Google, Adobe, and Amazon faculty awards. eugenewu.net









Josh Pollock is a recent PhD graduate from the VIS group at MIT, advised by Arvind Satyanarayan. His research applies programming language ideas to visualization grammars, with a particular focus on finding unifying abstractions across domains. Josh’s work starts with the hypothesis that there is a universal, extensible language for data-driven graphics analogous to the lambda calculus or relational algebra. His research systems include GoFish and Bluefish, which unify UI, chart, and diagram abstractions; Animated Vega-Lite, which unifies interaction and animation for charts; and Benthic, which unifies abstractions for chart and diagram accessibility. joshmpollock.com

title: Accepted Submissions
text:
Presented at the Workshop
Six of the accepted papers will be presented as talks on November 9, 2026 (see the schedule).



  Mind Your νs and Qs: A Categorical Framework for Specifying Visualization Components
  Hannah Aizenman, Mikael Vejdemo-Johansson, Thomas Caswell, Michael GrossbergCUNY Graduate Center; CUNY College of Staten Island; Brookhaven National Laboratory; City College of New York
  PDF
  
    Abstract
    Graphical grammars express how to put visual elements together; we propose a methodology for defining those visual elements in a manner that guarantees that they are structure preserving. Fiber bundles provide a uniform interface for describing a variety of data (tables, images, networks, etc.) in a manner that independently encodes the mathematical structure of the continuity and fields of the dataset. Modeling the data containers that store the datasets as sheaves provides a framework for specifying visualization methods that are designed to work regardless of how the dataset is stored, whether on disk, distributed, or on demand. Specifying the visualization library components as natural transforms of sheaves means that the constraints that the component must satisfy to be structure preserving can be specified as the set of morphisms on the data and graphic sheaves, including the structure on the continuity and fields of the data. Formally expressing how visual elements are constructed using category theory means we can translate those constraints into pseudocode, which can be used to implement the words in the visual sentence in a way that ensures that the sentences generate images that are faithful translations of the data.

  



  On the Inconsistency in Grammar Evaluations
  Lemara WilliamsWashington University in St. Louis
  PDF
  
    Abstract
    Current evaluation methods for visualization grammars are fragmented and inadequate. This work explores the community's lack of a standardized approach to evaluating grammars and comparing them. We propose broadening the evaluation criteria to include metrics like ease of use, conciseness, expressivity, and more rigorous evaluation techniques.

  



  Balancing constriction and expansion for domain-specific grammars
  Jason Cory BrunsonLaboratory for Systems Medicine, University of Florida
  PDF
  
    Abstract
    Graphical grammars distinguish from heuristic typologies in constituting closed formal systems whose product diversity arises from recombination rather than from de novo redesign. In practice, the scope of an implementation is constrained both by what options have been implemented for each component (e.g. the polar coordinatization, the grouped count statistic, and the rectangle geometric element) and by what combinations are enabled (these three yielding a pie graphic). In the interest of flexibility, implementations are generally permissive of syntactically valid combinations. However, within some domains, universal or conditional rules may be in place to ensure that graphics faithfully communicate important properties of the input data, such that permitting violations would compromise their integrity. I will present geometric data analysis as a motivating case study for this situation. Visualizations of point clouds, and especially the use of biplots, relies universally on a unit aspect ratio and conditionally on coordinate standardization for plot elements to approximate geometric relationships among data elements. Rather than a limitation of graphical grammar, these should be viewed as opportunities to explore the phrase spaces of different graphical domains. Indeed, the geometric constraints above enable the meaningful use of two families of statistical transformation (projections of constructions in higher dimensions and constructions in relation to referent points) that would otherwise produce uninterpretable graphics. This leads me to argue for a change in language from Wilkinson's assertion that, while a grammatical system can produce hideous graphics, it cannot produce meaningless ones. I suggest that meaningfulness and meaninglessness are not mathematical properties secured by formal rules but semantic properties vested with cultural significance, and that graphical grammars must adapt to the culture of a domain in order to serve as trustworthy tools for communicating information within it.

  



  The Grammar of Graphics Needs Verbs: Towards a GUGOG
  Josh M. PollockIndependent Researcher
  PDF
  
    Abstract
    The Grammar of Graphics (GoG) made significant strides toward unifying previously incompatible chart abstractions into a shared conceptual model. Today, we face a related problem. Inspired by the GoG, we have a proliferation of domain-specific grammars whose compositional ideas are difficult to compare and combine. I argue that one source of this divergence is that while the GoG gives us a powerful set of nouns for statistical graphics (marks), it provides no equally general set of verbs for composing marks together. Through this lens, we can understand recent grammars as specialized extensions of the GoG with verbs for arranging, compositing, repeating, or otherwise relating marks to each other. But because each grammar introduces these operations in its own language, closely related ideas are still difficult to compare, combine, and carry into practice. In this position paper, I show how the GoFish grammar's relations and operators can represent three recent grammars in a shared system. GoFish allows the same verbs to be used across all three systems, making it easier to compare and contrast grammars and identify their core contributions.

  



  Semantic Validity vs. Graphical Arrangement in Visualization Grammars
  Cynthia A. Huang, Matthew KayLMU Munich and Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML); Northwestern University
  PDF
  
    Abstract
    Systems for modular, declarative and compositional specification for data visualizations, otherwise known as visualization grammars, often claim Wilkinson's Grammar of Graphics as motivation, inspiration or foundation. However, despite the shared intellectual lineage, visualization grammars can vary greatly in design scope and focus. In particular, systems that strongly adhere to domain-specific notions of correctness must trade-off expressivity for validity. This trade-off between semantics and graphical flexibility is currently under-articulated, leading to difficulty integrating various GoG-inspired visualization contributions, especially between InfoVis and Statistical Graphics. We propose three new types of visualization contributions to support such integration: Semantic Validity Theories, Semantic Visualization Systems and Graphical Arrangement Systems. The first two prioritize the adherence of data visualizations to correctness conditions, such as statistical or mathematical transformations and data semantics, whilst the third largely leave validity concerns to the user. We illustrate these new contribution types using examples from two recent grammar of graphics inspired papers, and show how they supported more nuanced notions of expressivity and usability in evaluation and design of visualization systems.

  



  Can the Grammar of Graphics Describe Data Glyphs? Exploring the Application of the Grammar
  Barbara Nascimento, João M. Cunha, Evgheni PolisciucInstitute for Interdisciplinary Research, University of Coimbra; CISUC/LASI, University of Coimbra
  PDF
  
    Abstract
    The Grammar of Graphics (GoG) provides a formal and compositional framework for describing how data are transformed into graphical representations. Although grammar-based approaches have been widely applied to conventional visualisations, their applicability to data glyphs has not been fully explored. Data glyphs are composite visual entities that encode multiple data dimensions within a single graphical object and may employ heterogeneous visual elements, mapping strategies, and internal layouts. This work investigates whether the GoG can serve as a foundation for the grammar-based generation of data glyphs. We conduct a theoretical analysis of the GoG layers and apply them to two representative glyphs with distinct structural characteristics: a star glyph and a Chernoff face. The comparison indicates that the star glyph can be described through a relatively direct application of the original layered pipeline. In contrast, the composite structure of the Chernoff face requires component-specific mappings and suggests the need for an iterative application of the graph layers followed by an explicit graphical composition mechanism. These findings indicate that the GoG provides a useful foundation for describing data glyph construction but may require adaptations to support heterogeneous components and complex internal layouts. This work constitutes an initial theoretical investigation and provides directions for future grammar-based approaches to data glyph generation.

  Towards a natural language interface for graphic grammars and for specifying visualisation types
  Yuri Engelhardt, Clive RichardsUniversity of Twente; Birmingham City University
  PDF
  
    Abstract
    We propose a system for generating natural language sentences that can be used to describe the declarative, modular and compositional aspects of visualisation grammars, and to specify visualisation types, while being accessible to people who have no acquaintance with formal syntax or coding. The system builds on 'The Languages of Visualisation', which also includes Gestalt aspects of visualisations, and has in turn informed recent systems such as BlueFish and GoFish.

title: About
text:
Declarative, modular and compositional approaches to the specification of visualizations—otherwise known as graphical or visualization grammars—often claim Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics as motivation, inspiration, or foundation. Despite the shared intellectual lineage, visualization grammars encompass a broad array of different abstractions, primitives, and compositional strategies, along with a diversity of target users and usage scenarios.
The design goals and implementation sophistication of graphical grammars also vary greatly. The popularity of open-source visualization grammars such as ggplot2, Vega-Lite, and Observable Plot amongst different user bases, coupled with differences in their approaches to operationalizing Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics, gives rise to questions about what makes a grammar system successful and how evaluation methods can reflect multi-faceted success criteria.
Our current conceptualization and evaluation of grammar-based approaches lacks comprehensive integration of these differences and nuances. Existing commentary is fragmented across multiple research and practitioner communities—spanning visualization, statistical graphics, and programming languages research—making systematic review difficult.

title: About
text:
Workshop Goals
This workshop aims to seek a unified view of the diverse application contexts, functional goals, and design philosophies embedded in the proliferation of grammar-based visualization tools. While IEEE VIS regularly features papers on individual visualization systems and grammars, it rarely provides structured opportunities for cross-system comparison, meta-theoretical reflection, community consensus building, and practitioner perspectives.

Intellectual Integration — The field lacks comparative frameworks for understanding similarities, differences, and complementarity across grammar systems. We will examine functional requirements and features of graphical grammars beyond narrow evaluation criteria such as cognitive dimensions of notation.
Bridging Theory and Practice — Many practitioners struggle to choose between grammar systems or adapt them for novel visualization challenges. We hope to develop practical guidance for both tool builders and users, and to explore issues of learnability and adoption, including opportunities for natural language interfaces to lower the barrier to entry.
Community Building — Bringing together researchers working on different grammar systems—from ggplot2 extensions to Vega-Lite variants to novel formalisms—will foster cross-pollination across CS and statistics communities and potentially collaborative efforts toward more unified approaches.

The intended outcome is a cohesive interdisciplinary research agenda for grammar-based approaches in visualization research, with plans for follow-up initiatives such as an associated event at JSM 2027 and summary notes published on this website.

title: About
text:
Organizers
GUGOG is co-organized with the Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML), the joint AI research center of LMU Munich and TU Munich, which also supports the workshop.






Cynthia Huang is a postdoctoral researcher at the Social Data Science and AI chair at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, Germany, working on data preparation and visualization tools that incorporate statistical, computational, and usability considerations. Her related work includes a novel graph-based workflow grammar for data harmonization, a grammar-based system for extracting canonical tables from spreadsheets, and time-aware grammar of graphics geometries. She was co-chair of WOMBAT 2025 and will be a panellist at the ggplot2 session at JSM 2026. cynthiahqy.com









Matthew Kay is an Associate Professor jointly appointed in Computer Science and Communications Studies at Northwestern University. He works in human-computer interaction and information visualization, with a particular focus on uncertainty visualization and visualization literacy. His work includes a probabilistic grammar of graphics, the widely-used ggdist R package for uncertainty visualization, and studies of how data analysts use visualization grammars in practice. He organized a SIG on visualization grammars at CHI 2021 and co-directs the Midwest Uncertainty Collective.









Susan Vanderplas is an associate professor in Statistics at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. She researches data visualization, reproducible computing, and machine learning algorithms for forensic pattern matching. Her related work includes the animint package for extending ggplot2 to interactive graphics, and contributions to ggpcp for parallel coordinate plots. srvanderplas.github.io









Heike Hofmann is Professor of Methodology in Observational Data and Exploratory Data Analysis in the Department of Statistics at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. She is interested in tools and methodology for visualizing large, multivariate, and complex data. She co-founded the Graphics Group, a network of almost 100 members interested in statistical graphics, established in 2002. Her prior work includes numerous ggplot2 and grammar of graphics extensions.









Joyce Robbins is a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Statistics at Columbia University. Her main interests are data visualization and statistics education, with current work focused on mapping the ggplot2 extension package ecosystem. She is an active member of the Statistical Graphics Section of the American Statistical Association and has organized sessions on interactive graphics and ggplot2 extension packages at JSM. github.com/jtr13









Evangeline Reynolds is a data scientist and educator focused on tools that make data analytics more fluid and intuitive. Her ggplot2 extension contributions include ggcirclepack, ggregions, and ggdims. She works in developer relations for the ggplot2 extender community at Posit PBC, co-founded and organizes the ggplot2 extenders club, and developed the ‘easy geom recipes’ and ‘express’ educational resources for ggplot2 extension. github.com/EvaMaeRey

title: GUGOG @ IEEE VIS 2026
text:
Call for Submissions: GUGOG Workshop @ IEEE VIS 2026 (Deadline Aug 1)
Dear Colleagues,
We invite you to submit your work to the Grand Unified Grammar of Graphics (GUGOG) workshop, a half-day hybrid workshop held at IEEE VIS 2026.
We welcome contributions from researchers working on programming languages, domain-specific languages, type systems, formal methods, and related areas who are interested in the foundations and design of grammar-based visualization systems. Systems such as ggplot2, Vega-Lite, and Observable Plot share intellectual roots in Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics, yet differ substantially in their type systems, compositional semantics, abstraction layers, and execution models. The workshop provides a structured forum for cross-system comparison, formal analysis, and community consensus building.
Submission Guidelines: We are seeking original, unpublished, or ongoing work on topics including, but not limited to: - Formal and algebraic semantics of visualization grammars - Type systems, compositionality, and correctness guarantees for visual encodings - DSL design, embedding strategies, and compiler/interpreter approaches - Comparative analyses of grammar-based systems and their abstractions - Domain-specific grammars (e.g., for ML pipelines, scientific data, geospatial) - Natural language interfaces and LLM-driven chart generation - Learnability, adoption, and practitioner experience
Submission Types: - Short position papers (< 4 pages) — conceptual or technical arguments; formal treatments, DSL critiques, and cross-paradigm comparisons welcome - Discussion abstracts (≤ 500 words) — provocations, open problems, and observations
All submissions are non-archival and not anonymous. Accepted work will be hosted on the workshop website, and authors are encouraged to reuse content in follow-up publications.
Important Dates: - Call Opens: May 15, 2026 - Submission Deadline: August 1, 2026 - Notifications: September 1, 2026 - Camera-Ready: October 7, 2026
Submission Link: https://new.precisionconference.com/vgtc → Select the VIS 2026 GUGOG track
For full details on submission guidelines and the workshop program, please visit the workshop website: https://gugog-vis.github.io/2026/
We look forward to your contributions and to seeing you at IEEE VIS 2026!
